situation:
You and your partner are the customer relations manager and the service operations manager at MERIDIAN AUTO GROUP, a used vehicle dealership group with four lots in the region. The founder and owner (judge) built the group from a single lot and is preparing to step away from the business next spring. The owner (judge) has asked the two of you to recommend how the group should handle a customer commitment it can no longer easily keep.

MERIDIAN AUTO GROUP sells pre-owned vehicles and runs its own service bays behind each lot. Used inventory has grown scarce and expensive at auction, and dealers who can secure vehicles at a predictable wholesale price hold a real advantage over those bidding car by car. Buyers, in turn, choose Meridian largely because the building that sells them a vehicle also repairs it.

Last quarter the owner (judge) signed a five-year agreement with COLUMBIA VEHICLE PROTECTION, a distributor that supplies both wholesale inventory and extended service contracts. The pricing that makes the agreement worth having rests on an exclusivity clause: Meridian may sell only Columbia service contracts, and Meridian's bays may perform contract repairs only for Columbia. A single, exclusive supply relationship also makes the group simpler to value when the owner (judge) puts it on the market.

About nine hundred customers still hold service contracts Meridian sold for HARBOR POINT WARRANTY before the change. Each of those contracts states in writing that covered repairs will be performed at a Meridian service bay. Service advisors have started turning those customers away at the counter, and complaints have reached the owner (judge) directly, several of them from repeat buyers who have bought three and four vehicles here.

The owner (judge) wants a recommendation on which obligation Meridian will honor, how it will be explained at the counter, and how the group will confirm customers received notice. Sending those customers to independent shops and reimbursing every claim spends cash the owner (judge) is counting on before the sale, and tells long-standing buyers to take their repairs elsewhere. Servicing them in Meridian's own bays while asking Columbia for a written exception risks a breach finding and the wholesale pricing Meridian's margins rest on.

You will present your recommendation to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendation and have answered the owner's (judge) questions, the owner (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are to assume the role of the founder and owner (judge) of MERIDIAN AUTO GROUP. Business background is the same as the situation above. You signed the exclusive agreement with COLUMBIA VEHICLE PROTECTION yourself, and you intend to step away from the business next spring. Complaints from long-standing buyers holding HARBOR POINT WARRANTY contracts have come to you directly.

You want the customer relations manager and the service operations manager to recommend which obligation Meridian will honor, to explain how that decision will be presented to customers at the counter and over the phone, and to describe how the group will confirm that its notice actually reached the contract holders.

During the course of the role-play you are to ask the participant team the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What should a service advisor say to the first Harbor Point customer who walks in tomorrow morning?
How will we know the customers holding those contracts actually received our notice?
